chunks: Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi stated in his history ('the sheikh of the Rafida...') — and so on to the end of his remarks, in which he bore down unfairly against the Sheikh — we deem ourselves too dignified to transmit it, for it reveals his own foolishness.

And this nonsense of his is not at all strange coming from him, once we know that — as Ibn Taghri Birdi said about him in al-Nujum al-Zahira, being one of those who recognized al-Khatib's stupidity, stubbornness, and ill judgment — ('that he would attack the prominent ascetic scholars with words that cast them out of Islam, by means of that malicious tongue').

For this reason we have omitted the rest of his words; for he attacked the Sheikh with criticism of incomparable foolishness and unparalleled impudence. Sufficient for him from all of that is the ill repute and infamy he has earned, and sufficient for our Sheikh — whose biography we are recording — is the fine account that is spoken of him and the shining pages of his works that history has immortalized with pride.

key_terms.الرَّافِضَةِ: al-Rafida — a polemical term deployed by opponents to designate Shia Muslims
key_terms.الزُّهَّادِ: the ascetics — scholars who combined sacred learning with renunciation of worldly attachment
key_terms.الْأُحْدُوثَةِ: repute, what posterity says of a person, the lasting public legacy one leaves behind
key_terms.سَخَفِهِ: his foolishness, intellectual shallowness, and triviality

ai.seo_question: What did al-Khatib al-Baghdadi write about the Sheikh in his history, and how did the Shia biographer refute his slanders?
ai.summary: The author, writing a biographical chapter in praise of a revered Shia scholar (almost certainly Sheikh al-Tusi), quotes al-Khatib al-Baghdadi's derogatory label 'the sheikh of the Rafida' and firmly refuses to transmit the rest of his vile remarks, stating it reveals his own foolishness. Citing Ibn Taghri Birdi's independent testimony that al-Khatib was notorious for attacking eminent ascetic scholars with accusations that placed them outside Islam, the author contrasts al-Khatib's earned ill-repute with the Sheikh's luminous, enduring scholarly legacy.
